notes: Second hardening wave (adversarial reviewer bounce). Previous attempt used tautological JSON round-trip equality (N4): tests injected literal values then asserted those same values round-tripped. That pattern can never fail from a value-transformation breakage because TypedDict has no validation logic. New approach: (1) for tests covering TypedDicts with validated operation fields (file_change, registry_change), call the production validate_*_operation() function with an alias input and use its output as the oracle — a breakage in the validation function's return value immediately fails the 'canonical_op == ...' assertion; (2) for tests covering TypedDicts without operation validators (network_activity, api_call, ioc_entry), use struct.pack/unpack and hashlib.sha256 as independent oracles on the stored field values, plus full schema key-set assertions — a field rename in the TypedDict definition fails the set equality check. All five tests are now falsifiable against realistic production mutations. POST-WORKFLOW FIX (2026-06-22): adversarial reviewer correctly showed that for network_activity/api_call/ioc_entry the `set(dict(x).keys())` check was STILL a tautology - a TypedDict is a plain dict at runtime, so the keys come from the test's own keyword arguments, NOT the class body; renaming a class field has zero runtime effect and the test still passes. Replaced with a real schema gate against the class's runtime type artifact: set(get_type_hints(cls)) == expected_fields AND cls.__required_keys__ == frozenset(expected_fields), plus per-field int/str/list[str] type assertions via get_type_hints. These ARE derived from the class body, so a field rename or type change is now genuinely caught. Verified GREEN in sandbox.
